title: AI shaming has a moment: 'Daggermouth,' that Atlantic piece, and the BookTok backlash
text:
AI shaming has a moment: 'Daggermouth,' that Atlantic piece, and the BookTok backlash
An AI detector says a novel is riddled with AI-written work. The author denies it. Another career hangs in the balance—but this time readers are rising up to defend the work.
When last we checked in on the literary world’s AI battles, the publisher Hachette had cancelled the release of the novel Shy Girl due to concerns about the author’s use of AI. Remember that? Seems like years ago.
It was March.
This week another dustup dusted up in ye olde groves of literature. Will Oremus, the Atlantic staff writer who’s done groundbreaking work on AI and copyright theft, posted an explosive piece last week that accused H.M. Wolfe, author of the #1 bestselling sci-fi romance Daggermouth, of using AI to write the book.
Oremus didn’t do it directly. Rather, he quoted a forthcoming study that ran 14,000 Kindle ebooks through the AI detection tool Pangram. As Oremus reported:
One in five came back as more than 25 percent AI-written; Daggermouth returned 60 percent, according to an underlying data set that the authors shared with me. Those numbers, they acknowledge, tell us only so much. The researchers grouped together text that Pangram had flagged as either “AI-generated” or “moderately AI-assisted” (the latter of which can mean that AI was used to edit or polish human writing, or vice versa). And although Pangram has a low rate of false positives, it is
[not perfect].
The study’s lead author, Stony Brook University computer science professor Tuhin Chakrabarty, followed up with a secondary test. He and his co-authors scanned each book for “rare expressions”—strings of at least five words in a specific order—that also appear in other suspected AI books but almost never in human-written ones.
Oremus reported:
Daggermouth had many of them. For instance, the following sentence appears near the end of a multipage sex scene in Chapter 27: “They collapsed together, a tangle of sweat-slicked limbs and racing hearts.” That same sentence, word for word, also shows up in another self-published ebook by a different author. Or consider this line from Chapter 38 of Daggermouth: “Her pulse thundered in her ears, drowning out the murmurs of the crowd.” It’s also in an ebook by another author who has published more than 400 different titles on Amazon in the past three years.
Wolfe, the author, vehemently denied the accusation. She told The Atlantic: “I wrote this book myself. I have been outspoken about my opposition to generative AI and what it’s doing to writers, artists, and the creative community. I don’t believe it belongs in the writing process.”
“To be clear, there is no definitive proof that Wolfe used AI,” Oremus wrote.
BookTok strikes back
Fans of Daggermouth, many of whom are BookTop influencers, lashed back. “I don’t think I’m exaggerating in the use of the word ‘enraged,’” wrote Ed Lee, who collected a number of examples on his always-prescient site ChatGPT Is Eating the World.
Influencers like Emma Skies, above, accused Oremus of witch-hunting, racism, sexism, click-baiting, and a basket of other sins. Take their reaction as a marker of the metastasizing growth and clobbering power of AI shaming. They, more than most, know that the slightest hint of AI use is enough to destroy an author’s career right now.
Much as I loathe the Amazon-fueled growth of AI-slop Kindle books, I think the BookTok’ers land some solid punches. The Atlantic headline slams Daggermouth as AI slop while the article’s “no definitive proof” disclaimer appears six paragraphs deep in ten-point type. That smells a little push-poll-ish.
Is anyone actually lying?
H.M. Wolfe says she doesn’t use AI. The Pangram tool says she does. Either Wolfe is lying or Pangram flagged her as a false positive. Or maybe something in between?
You don’t have to search far to find queries into Pangram’s false positive rate (about 1 in 10,000, Pangram officials claim). It’s helpful to remember that AI detectors like Pangram are AI. They operate by ingesting the same mass of data that all AI models ingest. There is a world where data scrapers ingested Daggermouth even as Wolfe was writing it, regurgitated phrases to other users, who then published those phrases in their own work, which caused Pangram to double-back on Wolfe. This is actually happening to a number of songwriters these days.
Wolfe also may be using the same centuries-old techniques all writers have used, which is to jot down melodious words and phrases as she comes across them in her own reading, and later call them up from memory for use in an apt spot in her own developing manuscript. It happens all the time.
She might also have used AI to edit the manuscript, with the machine nudging her organic phrases ever so slightly into alignment with what the AI model categorizes as better writing.
Or…Wolfe’s novel is actually riddled with AI. According to Goodreads, the author’s first Kindle ebook, The Book of Cin, was published March 6, 2025. Her second, Blood Rains Down, came out roughly three months later. Her third, Daggermouth, was released last December.
Three novels in one year. Joyce Carol Oates thinks that’s a lot. There may be reasons. Wolfe may have been writing for years, drawer-keeping the novels until she finally decided to take a chance with Amazon’s ebook program. But. But. But.
Relax, you’re soaking in it.
Pangram and other AI detectors aren’t ubiquitous, but they’re increasingly used to scan student work, legal documents, creative manuscripts, and other writing. Substack recently installed Pangram as a feature akin to spellcheck. Last week I happened to run it on my own “Call in the philosophers” post.
I passed.
What if I hadn’t? Would I then be locked into battle with a machine over the organic nature of my own words? To whom would I appeal? What evidence could I offer?
Given the hair-trigger nature of AI accusations right now, honestly I’d probably rewrite the post or abandon it altogether. It’s not worth the fight. Simply by engaging with such an accusation, I’d lose. My name would be smeared with AI slop.
Hed: Was this author’s Substack about AI written by AI?
Text: Hard to say. An accusation has been made, but we can’t be sure either way. To be clear, there is no definitive proof that Barcott used AI.
